title: Lesson 8: Designing Tools That Fail Well: Schemas, Error Handling, and Retries
description: A tool is an operational contract, not an API wrapper. This lesson covers the five-part anatomy of a production tool, structured error schemas the model can act on, and retry discipline (backoff with jitter, idempotency keys, and retry budgets), so agents survive failures without corrupting state.

questions.question: What does it mean to treat a tool schema as an operational contract?
options: It defines the inputs, outputs, and error path
It locks the tool to a single model provider
It documents the tool only for human developers
It removes the need to validate arguments at runtime
questions.explanation: The schema is the agreement among the model, your application, and the backend, and its error path is part of that agreement rather than an afterthought.

questions.question: Why is the description field so important in a tool schema?
options: It sets the token price charged for the call
It tells the model when to use the tool and when not to
It encrypts the arguments before execution
It determines where the tool appears in the available list
questions.explanation: The description is what the model reasons over when choosing a tool, so covering when not to use it prevents the model from reaching the tool in the wrong situation.

questions.question: A write tool times out after the server already processed the request. What prevents a retry from duplicating the operation?
options: An exponential backoff with full jitter
A retry budget shared across the turn
An idempotency key that returns the first result
A circuit breaker that pauses traffic to the failing provider
questions.explanation: An idempotency key lets a retry return the first result instead of executing the write again, which is why state-mutating tools must be safe to repeat.
